articles.title: ‘Pakistan Idol’ in dark times
articles.content: WATCHING the long-awaited finale of Pakistan Idol was a refreshing break from the country’s ongoing political turmoil and escalating regional tensions. It was a fascinating contest between half a dozen exceptionally talented young amateur artists from across Pakistan, selected from hundreds of contestants — many from the remotest corners — who had competed for nearly a year. I was completely hooked, and followed every episode on television. What struck me most was the raw talent of these young performers — especially the girls from small towns, fiercely determined to prove themselves on the national stage. Hira Qaisar took the title of Pakistan Idol. A mother of three from Faisalabad who has never had any formal music training, she held the judges and audience spellbound with her mastery of both classical and popular singing. Hira was certainly exceptional; stars like her are born every season. That brilliance is in stark contrast to the hopelessness and frustration that young people feel today. With few opportunities and rising unemployment, they are leaving the country — many by illegal means, risking their lives in the hope of a better future. Hundreds die on the way and still they keep trying. It is hard to imagine a worse outlook for a nation where roughly 64 per cent of the population is under 30. Around four million people are added to the population every year, while 25m children are out of school, one of the highest numbers globally. Even among those enrolled, many can hardly read or write. The country is producing an ever-larger pool of undereducated, unskilled citizens. Youth unemployment is far higher than the national average. Pakistan is facing a severe youth crisis, and events like Pakistan Idol offer only a fleeting moment of pride. A youth bulge is a huge source of talent, but only if provided with education, jobs and a functioning state. Right now, it doesn’t have these. The system has failed to address the critical issues driving this crisis, and inaction has eroded young people’s belief that state institutions can deliver for them. We face a youth crisis of such severity that events like ‘Pakistan Idol’ are just a fleeting spark. Most disturbing of all is the collapse of the rule of law and the denial of basic democratic rights. An elite-dominated, extractive political system remains unresponsive to ordinary people, and the result is growing cynicism and radicalisation across society. What is unfolding in Balochistan, KP and Azad Kashmir is nothing less than a revolt of the youth against a repressive order and denial of basic democratic rights. The response of the state, which has relied on coercive force, has only aggravated the situation. Public discontent is growing, and it is tangible across the rest of the country as authoritarianism tightens its grip. New laws recently passed by parliament have further concentrated power in the hands of a single individual — ostensibly boosting the hybrid system. Yet such actions only render the system more vulnerable to implosion rather than strengthen it. It is a lesson of history we refuse to learn. Last week, we witnessed theblatant defianceof Supreme Courtinstructionsthat the imprisoned former prime minister Imran Khan be admitted to a private hospital for a full medical checkup. Khan was taken to a government hospital, not the one ordered by the court. While this defiance is read as a sign of hubris, it also exposes the fault lines within the hybrid system. A government of questionable legitimacy appears so afraid of popular backlash that it will not even allow the former prime minister to be admitted to a hospital for a medical checkup. There is also the question of whose decision it was to ignore the court order. The issue of Khan’s hospital transfer has now become a major flashpoint between the government and the opposition. In fact, it has divided the government itself. This is now a test for the Supreme Court, whose own independence has been drastically curtailed. In the past, prime ministers have been removed for defying the court’s orders. Can history be repeated? Many doubt it will be, given that the independence of the judiciary has already been compromised. But the incident has heightened political tensions in the country, and those who had bet on the fall of the government by the end of the year are now willing to raise the stakes. Given the historical unpredictability of Pakistani politics, one must not rule out any possibility, however far-fetched it may sound at the moment. Pakistan’s role in the emerging defence architecture of West Asia, defined by thenewly signed trilateral Makkah Joint Defence Pact, has certainly raised the country’s regional profile. But Islamabad’s ambition to become a net security provider carries the risk of overstretching its military. It also risks being drawn into a wider conflict, given the escalating tensions driven by America’s unending war on Iran. Pakistan has managed its balancing act well so far, but it could flip as President Donald Trump declares an economic war on Iran. There is also the question of whether a fragile economy can bear the burden of overextended defence commitments. America’s latest economic war on Iran could draw China into the conflict too. Beijing has warned that it would safeguard its interests after Washingtonlaid out plans for Iran’s “economic strangulation”. The statement came after the Trump administration threatened to impose penalties on countries, including China, if they breached the embargo. China is Iran’s biggest trading partner and has repeatedly stated that it firmly opposes illegal unilateral sanctions. “China will take all necessary measures to firmly safeguard its own rights and interests,” the country’s foreign ministry asserted in a statement. Any confrontation between the two superpowers could endanger Pakistan’s delicate balancing act, given Islamabad’s close ties with both. Considering its political and economic instability, Pakistan can hardly afford to become part of a conflict that can damage its national security. It is high time the hybrid rulers defused political tensions, rather than fuelled them, by pursuing a policy of vengeance. There is also a need to focus on the real issues that confront the country. Authoritarian measures have only increased the vulnerability of the existing political order.
articles.author: Zahid Hussain

articles.title: Who controls the answer?
articles.content: A NOTIFICATION appeared on some iPhones carrying theBBC Newslogo. Luigi Mangione, the man accused ofkillingUnitedHealthcare chief executive Brian Thompson in New York, had shot himself, it said. Except he had not. Mangione was alive and in custody. TheBBChad published no such claim. Apple Intelligence grouped threeBBCnotifications into a single summary and turned one into a false statement. Following complaints from theBBCand other news organisations, Apple temporarily suspended notification summaries for news and entertainment apps. The incident was widely treated as another AI error, but its implications went further. TheBBChad done the reporting, yet AI had changed what potentially millions of users thought it had reported. Its name remained on the alert even though it no longer controlled the information attached to it. Something similar is now happening on a much larger scale. People are turning to AI assistants with questions they once asked Google, journalists or experts, such as what happened in an election or why a war began. In all fairness, search engines were never neutral to begin with. They decided whether a report fromDawnappeared beside an obscure Indian website presenting itself as a research platform, and most users rarely moved beyond the first few results. But users could still open the original reports, see where each claim came from and judge the sources. AI removes that step. It reads the material, summarises it and presents its own version of what happened. This matters because malicious actors are already polluting the information space. Elections bring coordinated disinformation, synthetic audio and manipulated videos designed to promote candidates or discredit opponents. Governments and parties are no longer simply responding to news but producing their own version of events. People are turning to AI assistants with questions they once asked Google, journalists or experts, such as what happened in an election or why a war began. The same contest is visible in Gaza, where restrictions on journalists, competing claims and loaded language have shaped coverage. The killing of civilians, destruction of hospitals and homes, restrictions on aid and wider Israeli abuses are extensively documented, yet presented through radically different frames. Months of reporting by journalists, UN agencies and human rights groups may be placed against a single denial from the Israeli or US government. An AI assistant may then present both as equally credible, without showing how much evidence supports each account. The history of occupation may disappear, leaving what appears to be a dispute between two sides. The democratic danger is not limited to hallucination. It lies in allowing a handful of private companies to organise public knowledge. Citizens may receive one answer without knowing which newsroom established the facts, what evidence supports them or which accounts were left out. A confident summary can close a debate before the reader knows one exists. This is already happening. A study coordinated by the European Broadcasting Union and led by theBBCexamined more than 3,000 responses from four major AI assistants across 18 countries and 14 languages. It found that 45 per cent had at least one significant issue. Serious sourcing problems appeared in 31pc, while 20pc contained major accuracy issues. There is an economic consequence too. Traditional search normally preserved the click. Readers reached the news website, encountered the original reporting and generated some advertising or subscription value. AI systems can extract the result of that work, compress it into a paragraph and retain the user. Pew found that users were almost half as likely to click on a search result when an AI summary appeared. Publishers surveyed by the Reuters Institute expect search traffic to fall by 43pc over the next three years. Their reporting is still being used, but fewer readers are reaching the organisations that produced it. Large international publishers are negotiating licensing agreements with AI companies but smaller organisations have little comparable leverage. This is particularly dangerous for Pakistan, where journalism is already weakened by declining revenues, political pressure, delayed salaries and dependence on government and corporate advertising. Most publishers have no subscription base, limited technical capacity and little understanding of how often AI systems collect their work. The European Union has begun addressing parts of the problem. Its AI Act requires certain AI-generated or manipulated material, including deepfakes and unedited text on matters of public interest, to be labelled. Providers of general-purpose AI models must maintain copyright compliance policies and publish summaries of their training material. Systems designed to influence elections are treated as high risk, while the Digital Services Act requires the largest platforms and search engines to address risks to elections and civic discourse. But these protections do not settle the central question. They do not require an assistant to present several credible accounts, explain why it preferred one source, direct users prominently to the original report or compensate the publisher whose journalism supplied the answer. Pakistan needs to begin this discussion before the terms are set elsewhere. News organisations should measure AI crawling and referral traffic, decide how their archives may be used and bargain collectively with technology companies. Common agreements should require clear attribution, links to original reports, a process for correcting false summaries and fair payment when journalism is used commercially. Publishers must also rebuild direct relationships with audiences through memberships, newsletters and products that do not depend entirely on platforms. Journalism has lost audiences to new technologies before. This time, AI does not only decide which report is seen. It can rewrite the report, mix it with weaker sources and deliver the result without the reader reaching the newsroom. If these systems depend on reporting, they cannot be allowed to make the reporter disappear. The writer is the founder of Media Matters for Democracy.
articles.author: Asad Baig

articles.title: I spy, with…
articles.content: BEING a spy does not involve any special skills. Being a writer helps; being an artist is useful. What matters most is loyalty — to your own country, and sometimes to another above your own. The history of British espionage is crowded with spies with dual loyalties. For example, the Cambridge Five, a group of university undergraduates, were recruited by the Soviet NKVD in the 1930s and remained active until the 1950s. In 1951, two of them — Donald Maclean (codename Homer) and Guy Burgess — fled to the Soviet Union, followed in 1963 by a third, Kim Philby. A year later, a fourth, Sir Anthony Blunt (then Surveyor of the Queen’s Pictures), admitted to being a Soviet spy. Queen Elizabeth II was informed but advised to retain him, perhaps because years earlier, her father King George VI in 1945 had used Blunt (a former MI5 agent) in a secret mission in postwar Germany. Blunt was sent to retrieve the correspondence between Queen Victoria and her eldest daughter, the German empress Victoria, in case they fell into unscrupulous hands. Other unexpected spies included T.E. Lawrence (of Arabia), the novelist Graham Greene, Roald Dahl (a writer of children’s books), and the travellers Jan (formerly James) Morris and Nick Danziger. Both Danziger and Morris embellished their writings with sketches of the places they visited. Morris’ account of her stay in Pakistan is staid compared to the piquancy of Danziger’s Travels: Beyond Forbidden Frontiers (1987). In 1982, Danziger, after receiving a Winston Churchill fellowship of £1,000, journeyed overland through Iran, Iraq, Kurdistan, Afghanistan, Pakistan and China. He spent 18 months, journeying mainly “on foot, camel, horse and donkey”. Danziger had help from various agencies. In Paris, he contacted a Monsieur LeClerc — “a mine of information” — who provided him with crucial details about Afghan government strongholds, of Soviet bases, units of Afghan resistance, and the names of possible contacts. LeClerc scribbled these on a napkin which he folded and slipped into his own pocket. Much later, Danziger encountered him again in Peshawar where LeClerc was preparing to return to Afghanistan, on another “fishing expedition”. There’s a thin line between espionage, art and exploration. Danziger traversed Iran (then under Imam Khomeini), a volatile Iraq, dodged officialdom everywhere, and then aided by the Afghan mujahideen, he entered Pakistan via Chaman. En route, he took photos of locals and earned their goodwill (and money) by making “pretty poor” sketches which he sold. One is reminded of 19th-century itinerants like G.T. Vigne and August Schoefft who gained access to the Sikh court of Lahore by drawing flattering portraits of notables. Danziger lost his precious diary and cameras near the Afghan border. These were miraculously returned to him six weeks later. Danziger wanted to retrace the ancient Silk Route. By late 1984, he reached Khunjerab. Passing through scenery “so awesome and so forbidding”, he marvelled “at the magnificent arrogance of the engineers” who created a highway through it. After the Khyber, he felt disappointed to find the Khunjerab Pass “not a pass, but a wide open plain”. Those who have visited Khunjerab since Danziger might enjoy his description of that high-altitude border crossing: “Two pylons were separated by a frontier stone. The Pakistani pylon was smart, new and metal. The Chinese one was a cumbersome wooden pole.” Across the invisible border, he could see hundreds of yaks, guarded by Tajik shepherds on brown Bactrian camels. The Chinese immigration officers who examined Danziger’s passport couldn’t have been “friendlier”. They offered him first a chair, then an armchair, and finally a sofa. “Do you know,” they told an unsurprised Danziger, “that you are the very first foreigner to cross Khunjerab Pass?” Danziger’s subsequent journey through China tested his intrepidness. He defied prohibition by visiting ancient sites, stopped in Xian to admire phalanxes of terracotta warriors, made a foray into the inhospitable Taklamakan desert, and managed to secrete himself into Tibet and Bhutan. At the end of his arduous journey, Danziger, on re-entering the modern world, was made aware how escalation had overtaken him. Shopping in a village near Hong Kong, Danziger discovered that “the price of a paperback would have paid for one week’s board in China; the money for a cauliflower would have bought three meals in Peshawar”. Yet, when he returned to London, the frugal Danziger had some change left over from the £1,000 given to him by his Churchill Trust sponsors. On the second day after his return, Danziger, walking in London still wearing Afghan clothes, passed a van driver who shouted: “Nig-nog.” Throughout Asia, he had been welcomed as an inquisitive ‘white’ foreigner; at home, he found himself abused as a bearded immigrant.
articles.author: F.S. Aijazuddin

articles.title: Search for meaning
articles.content: EACH age has brought its own set of unique challenges. The present epoch is no different, as immense technological advances go hand in hand with widespread war, uncertainty and anxiety. We are witnessing the rise of machines with mind-boggling capabilities — superintelligence, they call it — while at the same time people seem to be losing their humanity, as the arrogant and the powerful bomb and maim innocent children, without facing accountability. We ask each other: what will tomorrow bring, what world will our children inherit? These anxieties are not limited to any one country, religion or race. It seems that most of humanity — at least ordinary people who have no role in perpetuating this bloodshed and chaos — is deeply concerned about what the future holds. Perhaps in these troubled times, when materialistic philosophies fail to offer any satisfactory explanations, the message that the Holy Prophet (PBUH), whose birth we celebrate today, brought over 14 centuries ago soothes the nerves and gives us some perspective: this world is transient, full of trials, and we will be made to answer for our deeds in the Divine court. This, arguably, is the core of the Quranic message and the Prophet’s Sunnah, and the crux of the message brought by all previous prophets. It explains that if the tyrants of today who spread chaos across the earth escape justice in this world, they will surely be brought before the Almighty tomorrow to answer for their crimes. As a hadith states, “the heavens and the earth stand upright by justice”. In the Noble Prophet’s life, we find examples of how to bring order to our personal and spiritual lives, as well as how to address society’s challenges. His message covered war and peace, periods of adversity and ease, how to live in the world and prepare for the hereafter. Regarding the transient nature of the world, Hazrat Ali relates that the Holy Prophet “took only that which he absolutely required from this world…”. This indicates that at all times — especially in these times of economic precarity — moderation and abstinence can help us weather the storm, as opposed to insatiable greed and the desire for more. In another hadith, the Noble Prophet is reported to have said: “My Lord has commanded me to be generous and do good and He has forbidden me from being stingy and from oppressing others.” This itself is a complete remedy to address society’s ills, as it emphasises helping others, doing the right thing and resisting oppression. This ties up perfectly with another tradition attributed to Hazrat Ali, where he says that “…whenever a destitute remains hungry, it is because some rich person has denied him his share”. These noble sayings point to the deadly sins — greed; oppression; injustice — that afflict our society, as well as the world at large. Some are power drunk, attacking others and threatening to lay to waste entire civilisations. In fact, their arrogant pronouncements echo the words of the tyrants the Quran has cited, such as pharaoh, Haman and Nimrood. Elsewhere, in societies like ours, which wear the outer garb of religion, the spiritual message of the Quran can hardly be found, as the weak and the oppressed continue to cry out for justice. Whether it is tyranny across the oceans, or turmoil within ourselves and our environs, if we refer to the hadith that states that “the world is the sowing field of the Hereafter”, things start to make sense. For example, if we ‘sow’ good deeds in this world — looking out for others, helping the weak and the voiceless, honouring the rights of God and man — we will ‘reap’ eternal peace in the next world. Conversely, and this brings comfort to victims of injustice, those who sow chaos on the earth will reap the harvest of their evil deeds in the world to come. In these times of uncertainty and immense global upheaval, it seems that patience (sabr) holds the key to success. After all, in the Holy Quran it is stated that “Allah is with the patient” (2:153). Meanwhile in hadith, those who bear afflictions with sabr are given glad tidings. But patience/sabr does not mean accepting injustice. As people of knowledge point out, it means rejecting all forms of oppression, staying the course and bearing internal and external hardships with fortitude. During his own blessed life, the Holy Prophet faced many different kinds of adverse circumstances, from the initial days of his mission in Makkah to the establishment of a state in Madina. But he dealt with all these challenges with help from the Divine, and immense strength of character. Therefore, the message is clear for believers; as the hadith states, they are grateful in prosperity, and patient in adversity. This formula can bring meaning to those searching for a direction in these times of trial.
articles.author: Qasim A. Moini

articles.title: Dual approach
articles.content: WITH regard to resolving the US-Iran stand-off, two distinct approaches are being pursued simultaneously. The more mature track involves Pakistan and other regional countries that are trying torevivetheIslamabad MoUand ensure a peaceful denouement to this crisis. In this regard, Chief of Defence Forces Field Marshal Asim Munir was in Tehran on Monday fortalks with the Iranian leadership. The other — more combative — approach involves the US ramping up financial pressure on Iran through sanctions and what it calls an “economic onslaught”. The US on Mondayannounceda fresh set of sanctions targeting Iran under the imaginatively titled ‘Operation Economic Outcast’. Field Marshal Munir met the Iranian president, as well as other top leaders, in Tehran. One of the positive outcomes of this interaction was Iran’s affirmation that it remains committed to the Islamabad MoU. However, as the Iranian national security chief said, “we distrust America”. This mutual distrust remains the biggest obstacle in operationalising the MoU. The reality is that America’s ramping up sanctions on Iran will do little to build bridges with Tehran. If anything, it will harden attitudes there. It should be remembered that Iran has survived punishing US sanctions for nearly half a century, and while the new curbs may increase the pain, they are unlikely to make Tehran yield. Moreover, there is little appetite amongst Iran’s major trading partners, particularly China, to toe Washington’s line. The announcement of new economic curbs is also an admission from the US that its strategy of defeating Iran on the battlefield has failed. The fact that the Iranians are willing to engage with mediators, and are still interested in reviving the Islamabad MoU, means that a peaceful way out of this crisis can be found. After the CDF’s visit, the Omani foreign minister was in Tehran yesterday to discuss the situation in the Strait of Hormuz. If the Trump administration goes ahead with its ill-advised plan to further isolate Iran economically, or if it considers restarting military action, it will undoubtedly attract a matching response from Iran. Very few states in the region want a return to hostilities. Therefore, both sides, particularly the US, need to take advantage of the renewed diplomatic push, and attempt to implement the salient features of the MoU. The US should drop its hostile rhetoric and attempt to reach a genuine understanding with Iran. Washington’s aggression against the Islamic Republic has proved a disaster, and it would be best for the US to quickly exit the quagmire with whatever remains of its tattered honour. The Iranians, meanwhile, should restore the free flow of marine traffic through Hormuz, and rebuild damaged ties with their Arab Gulf neighbours.
articles.author: Editorial

articles.title: Little to celebrate
articles.content: BY now it has become almost tedious to read the same assessment from every global credit rating agency and lender — Pakistan’s economy has stabilised, but risks remain. Moody’s commentary on the country’s economy accompanying its latest upgrade is simply a repetition of this review dressed up in a new number. And that tedium is itself the story: an economy that keeps producing the same verdict year after year is hardly holding steady; in fact, it is stuck. Macroeconomic indicators may not be falling, but nothing underneath them is moving either. Standing still while the rest of the world advances is nothing but a quiet form of decline. Moody’s new rating, still highly speculative and seven notches below investment grade, is not a vote of confidence. It is merely an acknowledgment that the country is marginally less likely to default than before. And yet it was an occasion for the prime minister to congratulate the nation as though we had turned the corner. This is the peculiar place Pakistani policymaking has settled into, where even minor technical adjustments are treated as milestones. The picture Moody’s has painted is unflattering. It points to a narrow export base, negligible FDI, heavy reliance on remittances, and a government that still leans on official and commercial borrowing to meet its external obligations. None of this describes an economy capable of standing on its own feet. It is being propped up by the IMF and rolled-over bilateral deposits. The governance language deserves more attention. The agency is blunt: weak rule of law, poor control of corruption, limited government effectiveness. These are not casual observations. These are the reasons investors continue to look elsewhere. Even the improvement in debt affordability that Moody’s highlights comes with a caveat. Interest payments have reduced substantially over the previous year. Yet the figure is so high that practically nothing is left for the social and infrastructure investment the country needs. This improvement is a function of falling inflation and rate cuts, not any structural change. What all of these add up to is an economy that has been stabilised in the technical sense but the deeper conditions for real growth remain elusive. Real recovery would have looked different. Moody’s upgrade is not a turning point; it is just a slightly better seat in the same waiting room.
